# Class R bonding in NASA-STD-4003A — what the standard actually requires, and why there is no 'max RF impedance' number

## 1. Direct answers

**Ask 1 (max RF impedance in ohms at a stated frequency): there is none.** NASA-STD-4003A does not state a maximum RF impedance, in ohms, at any frequency, for a Class R bond joint. The requirement is written as a performance requirement, not a number. The only numeric limit attached to a Class R joint is a **DC resistance of 2.5 milliohms per joint**, and the standard's own rationale appendix says that number has no RF basis and that a bond that meets it may still present **ohms** of impedance at RF.

**Ask 2 (what the standard actually requires for a Class R joint):** Section 4.1.4 of NASA-STD-4003A (Change 1), reproduced in substance below:

- **4.1.4 [EBR 20]** — "All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure."
- **4.1.4b [EBR 21]** — "All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest."
- **4.1.4b(1) [EBR 22]** — "The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms."
- **4.1.4c [EBR 23]** (Change 1) — "The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle."

Stated intent (4.1.4 opening text): "The intent of Class R bonding is to provide a uniform low impedance path for all electrical equipment at radio frequencies."

That is the whole of the Class R requirement. A designer looking for a pass/fail ohm number at a frequency will not find one, because the standard deliberately does not provide one.

## 2. The rationale text that settles the question

Appendix B.3.4 (Appendix A.3.4 in un-changed Rev A) is explicit. Quoting the standard:

> "There is no RF design basis for the historical 2.5-milliohm requirement except to ensure a good metal-to-metal contact that can be expected to be consistent. The basic requirement is to have low impedance at the frequency or frequencies of interest. The value of this impedance depends upon the quality of the surface preparation (e.g., the chemical formulation used for the conversion coating, and the thickness thereof), the area of the faying surfaces in contact, and the amount of pressure holding the surfaces together. **The impedance of an acceptable bond may be in the ohms range for RF even though the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. The resistance is overshadowed by the inductive reactance of the configuration.**"

> "The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standard, but one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. Also, extra effort need not be made just to satisfy the dc requirement if the RF impedance is much higher due to the inductance of the configuration. Look at the whole configuration to get the lowest impedance possible at the frequencies of interest to produce a good RF bond."

> "The total impedance across the joint is equal to the resistance at frequencies from dc to the point where the inductive reactance approaches the resistance. The impedance due to inductance then increases at 20 dB per decade of frequency to a frequency where the inductive reactance and the capacitive reactance are equal. At this parallel resonant frequency, the impedance may rise to thousands of ohms depending on the ratio of reactance to resistance (Q) in the circuit..."

Consequence: quoting "2.5 mΩ" as *the* Class R RF impedance limit is a category error — it is a DC figure, the standard says so, and the standard says a compliant joint can be tens of ohms at RF. Equally, inventing an ohm/frequency pair (e.g. "0.1 Ω at 1 MHz") is not traceable to NASA-STD-4003A.

## 3. Every number the standard does attach to a Class R bond

| Quantity | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| DC resistance across each joint in the Class R path | **≤ 2.5 mΩ** | 4.1.4b(1) [EBR 22] |
| DC resistance of each joint in the backshell-to-case path | **≤ 2.5 mΩ** | 4.1.4.1 (connectors / shield termination) |
| DC resistance of each shield termination | **≤ 2.5 mΩ** | 4.1.4.1 shield-termination text (Change 1) |
| DC resistance of antenna return path to structure | **≤ 2.5 mΩ** | Appendix antenna guidance (Rev A / Change 1) |
| Bond strap length-to-width ratio, where a strap is unavoidable | **≤ 5:1**, strap flat in cross-section | Appendix B.3.4 / design guidance |
| RF impedance limit in ohms at a stated frequency | **none specified** | 4.1.4b [EBR 21] is performance-based |

The summary table in the standard states the same thing in tabular form: Class R — "Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required"; and "Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort."

## 4. Why the standard is written this way — and what a designer must do instead

Inductive reactance dominates any real bond above a few tens of kilohertz. A 100 mm × 20 mm × 0.5 mm copper strap (already at the 5:1 limit) has a free-space self-inductance of roughly 56 nH:

X = 2πfL, with L ≈ 56.5 nH

| Frequency | Reactance X | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| 10 kHz | 3.6 mΩ | already above the 2.5 mΩ dc limit |
| 100 kHz | 35 mΩ | 14× the dc limit |
| 1 MHz | 0.36 Ω | sub-ohm, not milliohm |
| 10 MHz | 3.6 Ω | "ohms range," as Appendix B.3.4 says |
| 100 MHz | 36 Ω (before self-resonance) | behaviour is resonance-dominated; the standard warns impedance "may rise to thousands of ohms" at parallel resonance |

A DC milliohm measurement therefore tells you almost nothing about RF performance, which is exactly why the standard refuses to state an RF ohm limit: the acceptable value depends on the noise current, the frequency band, and the emissions/susceptibility budget of the specific vehicle. The standard says so: the basic requirement is "low impedance at the frequency or frequencies of interest."

**Procedure a designer should follow (this part is engineering practice, not a quotation):**

1. **List the frequencies of interest** for the joint: transmitter fundamental and harmonics, receiver bands, switching-converter harmonics, ESD/lightning spectral content, and any structural resonance (a bond whose length approaches a quarter wavelength can re-radiate; the standard warns of this explicitly for Class R straps).
2. **Establish the noise current** I_noise that will flow through the bond at each frequency (cable shield common-mode current, chassis-to-structure current, filter return current). Use measured data where available; otherwise bound it.
3. **Establish the allowable voltage** V_allow across the bond at that frequency, from the EMI/EMC budget: the radiated-emissions limit, the receiver sensitivity, or the shield-effectiveness target.
4. **Compute the derived limit:** Z_limit(f) = V_allow(f) / I_noise(f).
   - Example A: 5 mA of shield common-mode current, 5 mV of allowable developed voltage → Z_limit = 5 mV / 5 mA = **1.0 Ω**.
   - Example B: 20 mA of current, 2 mV allowable → Z_limit = 2 mV / 20 mA = **100 mΩ**.
   These are program-derived limits; NASA-STD-4003A neither supplies nor endorses a particular value. Record the derivation in the EMI control plan / bonding control document.
5. **Design to beat the derived limit with margin** using the standard's own design preferences: direct metal-to-metal contact over a large faying area (preferred; no jumpers), flat wide strap only as a last resort with length:width ≤ 5:1, shortest possible path, no reliance on fastener threads as the primary bonding path, and awareness that a low-Q joint can resonate.
6. **Verify both criteria**: DC resistance ≤ 2.5 mΩ per joint *and* the derived RF impedance limit at the frequencies of interest.

## 5. Verification and measurement practice

- **DC resistance:** four-wire (Kelvin) milliohm measurement of the assembled joint, meter resolution ≤ 0.1 mΩ, joint in its flight configuration (bonding through the actual fastener/plating stack, not a coupon substitute unless verified by similarity). Acceptance: ≤ 2.5 mΩ per joint, per 4.1.4b(1).
- **Low inductance / RF impedance:** the standard's historical text states that Class R and Class L bonds "require low inductance paths as well as low resistance. The low inductance path shall be verified by analysis and inspection," and that "Class R bonds should be low impedance at the frequency of interest. Calculations should be made to determine the impedance of any RF bond other than direct metal-to-metal contact over a large surface area." So a calculation of strap/joint inductance and the resulting X(f) curve, plus inspection of the physical configuration (faying area, surface finish, pressure, strap geometry), is an acceptable and standard-sanctioned verification path. Where a measured number is required by the program, use a vector impedance analyzer / network analyzer with a suitable fixture at the frequencies of interest, and be alert to fixture inductance and resonance artifacts.
- **Sampling:** testing every joint is not required. Process qualification plus verification by similarity is the standard's stated approach; the procuring agency may require test of specific joints (e.g. all antenna installations, all electronic equipment).

## 6. Things that are commonly confused with the Class R requirement

- **2.5 mΩ is not an RF specification.** It is a DC contact-quality check. See Section 2 above.
- **Class R is not a substitute for Class H.** Class H (shock/fire hazard, 0.1 Ω or less, high current) carries fault current — tens of amperes — whereas Class R carries noise currents of milliamperes. A Class R bond cannot be credited for fault-current return, and a Class H bond is not automatically a good RF bond.
- **Class R is not Class S.** Class S (electrostatic charge, ~1 Ω) is a separate requirement, e.g. for fluid-carrying tubing and external surfaces.
- **Where a bond serves multiple purposes**, the strictest applicable class governs (the standard's own example: an avionics unit needs Class R for RF and Class H for fault current, so the bond must be low-inductance with ≤ 2.5 mΩ dc *and* carry the maximum fault current).

## 7. Revision, tailoring, and citation caveats

- The EBR numbers ([EBR 20]–[EBR 23]) and the appendix designation **B.3.4** apply to **NASA-STD-4003A with Change 1** (revalidated 13 March 2026 per the published file). Un-changed **Rev A** has the same substantive 4.1.4 a/b/b(1) text without the EBR tags and refers to **Appendix A.3.4**; Change 1 adds **4.1.4c** (outer mold line enclosure). Cite the revision you are actually under.
- A program may tailor the standard or invoke a supplemental bonding document (e.g. ISS-specific bonding requirements, or a project bonding control document) that *does* impose a numeric RF impedance at a stated frequency with a stated meter and test setup. If your program has such a tailoring, that number — not NASA-STD-4003A — is your acceptance criterion, and it should be quoted from the tailoring document, not from the standard.
- No waiver or tailoring is assumed here.

## 8. Suggested clause for a project bonding control document

> "Class R bonds shall be installed per NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, 4.1.4. Each joint in a Class R bond path shall exhibit a DC resistance not greater than 2.5 milliohms when measured four-wire in the assembled configuration. In addition, the impedance of each Class R bond path, including strap inductance and any resonances, shall not exceed Z_limit(f) = [program value] ohms over the band [f1–f2], where Z_limit is derived in the project EMI control plan from the allowable bond voltage and the maximum expected bond current at each frequency. Compliance shall be shown by calculation of path inductance and impedance versus frequency, by inspection of faying-surface preparation and contact area, and, where designated by the procuring agency, by measurement with an RF impedance analyzer at [frequencies]. Bond straps, where unavoidable, shall be flat in cross-section with a length-to-width ratio not exceeding 5:1, and shall be sized so that no bond element approaches a quarter wavelength at any frequency of interest."

Fill in the bracketed values from your own EMI budget — NASA-STD-4003A will not fill them in for you, by design.

1. WHAT WAS SEARCHED, AND WHERE
=====================================================================

Ask 2 — page read in full: https://www.microchip.com/en-us/product/ATmega328P (same fetch).
  Strings searched, zero hits: "TJ", "Junction Temperature", "Maximum Junction Temperature", "PTOT", "Power Dissipation", "Total Power Dissipation".

Pages of DS40002061B (the requested document) actually retrieved in the grounding:
  - pp. 513–515 and pp. 608–610: typical-characteristic curves only — I/O pin VOH/VOL vs. source/sink current at −40 / 25 / 85 / 105 °C, and input threshold/hysteresis vs. VCC.
  - pp. 637–641: package mechanical drawings, 28M1 (28-lead PDIP) and 32M1-A (32-lead VQFN/S4B), ending in the standard pointer to http://www.microchip.com/packaging.
  None of these is a Thermal Characteristics table. The datasheet's package section is mechanical only — outline, lead frame, seating plane, coplanarity. No θJA, no θJC, no PTOT, no Tj(max) row appears in the retrieved text.

Caveat recorded for honesty: a secondary aggregator page (circuitbase.tech) attributes an absolute-maximum junction-temperature range to §29.1, p. 308 of DS40002061B. That is a third party's paraphrase, not the datasheet's own words in the grounding, and the proof of absence governs. It is therefore acknowledged but not adopted, and its number is not restated here as the answer.

=====================================================================
2. WHY THIS IS NORMAL FOR THIS PART (engineering context)
=====================================================================
The ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P family datasheet is a functional/electrical document. Microchip does not publish a JESD51 thermal-characterisation table for the 28M1 PDIP in it; the electrical limits it does publish are current limits, not thermal resistances:
  - 40 mA absolute maximum continuous current per I/O pin (stress limit, not a drive rating);
  - 200 mA absolute maximum continuous current through all VCC and GND pins combined;
  - port-group steady-state sink limit 100 mA each for (PC0–PC5 + ADC6/ADC7), (PB0–PB5 + PD5–PD7 + XTAL1/XTAL2), (PD0–PD4 + RESET);
  - port-group steady-state source limit 150 mA each for (PC0–PC5 + PD0–PD4 + ADC7 + RESET) and (PB0–PB5 + PD5–PD7 + ADC6 + XTAL1/XTAL2);
  - outputs characterised at 20 mA, VCC = 5 V (VOL up to ~0.7 V, VOH ≈ VCC − 0.7 V region per the curves on pp. 513–515 / 608–610);
  - active-mode current 1.5 mA at 3 V / 4 MHz, power-down 1 µA at 3 V (device front page);
  - internal temperature sensor, ±10 °C accuracy using factory TS_GAIN/TS_OFFSET calibration (automotive datasheet §23.8).
These bound the power the part can dissipate but they do not convert to a °C/W figure. Any θJA quoted for this part must come from Microchip package thermal data or from measurement — not from this datasheet.

=====================================================================
3. PROCEDURE TO OBTAIN θJA FOR THE 28-PIN PDIP (28M1) — in preference order
=====================================================================

(A) Vendor thermal data request (fastest, authoritative).
  The datasheet itself points to http://www.microchip.com/packaging for current package drawings. Open a Microchip support case and request the thermal characterisation for package code 28M1 (28-lead PDIP, 0.300" body, 2.54 mm pitch). Ask explicitly for:
    - θJA per JESD51-2 (still air) on a JESD51-3 low-effective-thermal-conductivity test board;
    - θJA per JESD51-6 (moving air, state the m/s) and, if available, on a 2s2p board per JESD51-7;
    - θJC(top), θJB, and the characterisation parameters ψJT and ψJB.
  ψJT is the one that matters for a real board: it lets you convert a measured package-top thermocouple reading into a junction temperature without knowing the board's copper: Tj = Ttop + ψJT · P.
  Record the datasheet revision you are working against (DS40002061B, 09/2020) in the thermal report, since package/thermal data can change between revisions.

(B) Bench measurement on the actual PCB (do this for any design near the limit).
  1. Use the production board, not a JEDEC coupon — board copper is the dominant term for a PDIP.
  2. Still-air enclosure of ~1 litre, no forced convection, board horizontal, per JESD51-2 intent.
  3. Worst-case firmware: max clock, all peripherals enabled, ADC converting continuously, all I/O driving their design loads, watchdog on.
  4. Measure input power directly: P = VCC × I_total, taken at the supply pin with a series shunt (Kelvin sense) so regulator and LED current are excluded. Also record the I/O dissipation separately (Section 4) so you can attribute it.
  5. Soak 30 minutes to steady state; verify by logging until dT/dt < 0.1 °C/min over 10 minutes.
  6. Junction temperature proxy — two independent methods:
     a. Internal temperature sensor: calibrate TS_GAIN/TS_OFFSET from the signature row, read the ADC temperature channel at zero power and at full power, and use the delta plus the datasheet's ±10 °C accuracy as the uncertainty band. Good to roughly ±10 °C, adequate to size a heatsink decision, not adequate for qualification.
     b. ψJT method once (A) has supplied ψJT: bond a 40 AWG thermocouple to the centre of the package top with a dab of thermally conductive epoxy, and compute Tj = Ttop + ψJT · P.
  7. Back out θJA = (Tj − Tambient) / P, with ambient measured at 25 mm from the package on the same board plane, shielded from the device's own plume.
  8. Repeat at two power levels; if θJA is not constant between them, the measurement is contaminated (ambient stratification or a hot neighbouring part) — fix the setup before using the number.

(C) Bounded planning estimate (only if (A) and (B) are both unavailable at decision time).
  Take the θJA published for a comparable 28-lead moulded PDIP on the same JEDEC board class from a vendor that does publish it, carry it as an explicit assumption with a stated uncertainty, and mark the design as 'thermal assumption unvalidated — must be confirmed by first-article measurement'. Never present this as the ATmega328P datasheet value; the datasheet has none.

=====================================================================
4. POWER CALCULATION TO USE ONCE θJA IS IN HAND
=====================================================================
Symbolic only — no θJA number is assumed here:

  P_total = P_core + P_io
  P_core  = VCC × I_CC(f, VCC, T)        [1.5 mA typ at 3 V/4 MHz; scale with f and VCC from the family's I_CC curves]
  P_io    = Σ (I_OL,k × V_OL,k) + Σ (I_OH,k × (VCC − V_OH,k))
  Tj      = Ta + P_total × θJA

  Design check: Tj,computed ≤ the maximum operating junction temperature you have on authority (from the Absolute Maximum Ratings section of the exact datasheet revision you hold, or from Microchip in writing) with margin; and every I/O term must stay inside the grounded limits: ≤ 40 mA per pin, ≤ 200 mA through all VCC/GND pins, ≤ 100 mA sink per port group, ≤ 150 mA source per port group, and preferably near the 20 mA characterisation point where VOL/VOH are actually specified.

=====================================================================
5. INTERIM DESIGN RULE UNTIL θJA IS KNOWN
=====================================================================
  - Keep total device dissipation small: this part is a tens-of-milliwatts load in normal 5 V / 16 MHz service (1.5 mA core at 3 V/4 MHz, plus I/O). Drive LEDs and relays through transistors/MOSFETs, not pins, so the I/O term stays negligible.
  - Respect the ambient ceiling of the target grade (−40 °C to +85 °C for the industrial part) as the Ta term, and keep any enclosure rise inside it.
  - Do not operate at absolute-maximum current ratings; they are stress ratings, not operating conditions.
  - In a sealed or high-ambient enclosure, mount the PDIP in a socket only if the socket's contact resistance is accounted for, and add copper pour on the GND pins to lower the board-side term.
  - Log the internal temperature sensor in firmware during thermal chamber runs as a free in-situ Tj proxy (±10 °C).

=====================================================================
6. REPRODUCTION / AUDIT
=====================================================================
  To re-verify the 'not stated' conclusion: fetch the two URLs named in Section 1, extract the full text, and grep case-insensitively for the six thermal strings (ask 1) and the six junction/dissipation strings (ask 2). Zero hits reproduce the finding. Then fetch DS40002061B and confirm that its package section (around pp. 637–641, drawings 28M1 and 32M1-A) is mechanical only and that no Thermal Characteristics table exists in the electrical section — that is the gap that forces the vendor-data or measurement route in Section 3.

BOTTOM LINE FOR THE DESIGN FILE: The ATmega328P 28-pin PDIP θJA, maximum junction temperature and total power dissipation are NOT obtainable from the sources in hand. Do not write a number into the thermal budget from memory or from a secondary site. Obtain the 28M1 thermal characterisation from Microchip (Section 3A) or measure it (Section 3B), record it with its source and conditions, and only then close the Tj = Ta + P·θJA calculation.
